editorialNote.title: Community-facing note, not a timeline event
body: Thank you very much for reading this timeline.
Dance, as an art form, suffers from its volatile nature.
Scholars all over the world are trying to mitigate flaws in recent decades.
To us, Shufflers, being both a rave and a social media culture creates unique challenges that most people do not care about.
This timeline is a collaborative work built to provide a historically accurate, informative, digestible and trustworthy source about Shuffling history, its years and constant changes.
It has required years of research and verification so new Shufflers and enthusiasts can learn without major doubts.
Remember: it is an endless work in progress.
If you have information to add or change, contact the project so it can be updated.

timeline.title: Aciiiiiied !!!

points.text: The artwork connects early rave foundations and Shuffling to a style it calls UK Rave Stepping.
Dropfoot is given as local terminology and Foot Patrol as pioneers.
The Second Summer of Love and Manchester are identified as cultural breakthroughs.
Acid House, Breakbeat and Jungle form the musical context.
Leeroy Thornhill, from The Prodigy, is named as a major influence on Melbourne ravers.
Running Man becomes a global dance fad associated with Janet Jackson, MC Hammer and Vanilla Ice.

elements: Large UK flag, smiley icon, acid/rave graphics and early rave imagery.

timeline.title: Birth of Melbourne rave scene

points.text: The dance was called Stomping and is described in the artwork as Pre-Melbourne Shuffle.
The artwork links this movement to British dance styles, including Northern Soul.
Raves at the Docks warehouse, including Shed 14, helped anchor Melbourne's rave scene.

points.text: T-Shuffle became a principal move in the oldschool vocabulary.

timeline.title: From Underground to Underage, then Worldwide

points.text: Malaysian students in Melbourne learned to Shuffle and helped spread the culture in Malaysia.
The Malaysian scene reached a peak with local competitions and group choreography.
XES.CX is named by the artwork as one of the oldest online sources.
Hardsequence adopted the name Hardstyle Republic.
Hardstyle Shuffle trended across Australia and Malaysia.

timeline.title: Cutting Shapes

points.text: Cutting Shapes began being used in the UK for dance involving shapes made with the whole body.
The artwork contrasts this with Shuffling as a footwork-focused term.
The original London scene was led substantially by Black dancers.
The #IGOTSHAPES YouTube series documented the scene.

sources.label: The Guardian: London's deep-tech and shuffling scene

points.text: Names including Shapeshifting, UK Shuffle, House Shuffle and London Shuffle circulated.
Club restrictions and opposition to the dance became known as the Shuffle Wars.
VICE released a documentary report with testimony and footage from the scene.
The original UK Cutting Shapes scene began to fade.

sources.label: The Guardian: London's deep-tech and shuffling scene
